planting.note: Direct sow on the soil surface in early spring, since seed needs light to germinate, or plant divisions in spring in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: The wild Caucasus native behind the many named fernleaf yarrow cultivars such as 'Gold Plate' and 'Coronation Gold', Achillea filipendulina produces broad, flat-topped heads of tightly packed mustard-gold florets held on sturdy upright stems above finely divided, aromatic, gray-green foliage from early to midsummer. It is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, thriving in lean, poor soils where richer perennials struggle, and its long-lasting flower heads are a favorite for fresh and dried arrangements. Give it excellent drainage, since soggy winter soil is far more damaging than cold or heat, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and flower size. Deadhead spent heads to prolong bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; good drainage is essential to prevent crown rot over winter.

directions: Geum chiloense, native to Chile, is the straight species behind the classic scarlet and semi-double avens cultivars such as 'Mrs. J. Bradshaw' long grown in cottage gardens. It produces wiry, branching stems carrying bowl-shaped, brilliant scarlet-red flowers above a low mound of hairy, strawberry-like basal foliage from late spring into summer. Plants perform best with afternoon shade and consistent moisture in hot-summer climates, since they struggle and may die back when temperatures stay above 85F for extended periods. Deadhead regularly to prolong bloom and divide congested clumps every two to three years in early fall to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions, broken stem pieces, or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; this creeping species roots readily wherever a trailing stem touches soil.

directions: Sedum rupestre, the European species sold in named gold-foliage forms such as 'Angelina' and variegated sports like 'Lime Twister', is a low, trailing succulent with whorls of narrow, needle-like, blue-green leaves on creeping, mat-forming stems. In summer it sends up short clusters of small, star-shaped yellow flowers above the foliage, though it is grown mainly for its evergreen, textural groundcover effect. It thrives on neglect in lean, sharply drained, sandy or gravelly soil and rots quickly in rich or poorly drained ground, making it a natural fit for rock gardens, wall crevices, and green roofs. Trim back any leggy growth in spring to keep the mat dense and tidy.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the horizontal, tiered branching structure room to develop unpruned.

directions: The wild Asian species behind popular named selections and the f. tomentosum doublefile forms such as 'Mariesii' and 'Shasta', Viburnum plicatum carries rounded, ball-like clusters of all-sterile white flowers along strongly horizontal, tiered branches in mid-spring, the classic old-fashioned 'Japanese snowball' look distinct from the flat lacecap doublefile forms. Its distinctive layered branching structure gives the shrub striking architectural presence in the landscape even without pruning, and the coarse-textured, deeply veined leaves often take on bronze-red fall color. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since the species is less drought-tolerant than many other viburnums and suffers in compacted or dry sites. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood immediately after flowering, since next year's buds set soon afterward.

planting.note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring after hard frost danger passes, or in fall in mild-winter climates, into moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Rosa chinensis is the East Asian species behind the historic China rose cultivars such as 'Mutabilis' and 'Old Blush' that revolutionized Western rose breeding in the late 1700s by introducing repeat bloom and tea-scented fragrance into once-a-year-flowering European roses. The wild-type species itself bears clusters of single to semi-double, lightly fragrant pink to carmine flowers continuously from spring through frost on a twiggy, lightly thorned shrub with glossy, dark green foliage. It is exceptionally heat- and humidity-tolerant and more resistant to blackspot than many modern hybrid teas, making it a reliable choice where other roses struggle. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, since hard pruning sacrifices the continuous bloom this species is valued for.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; the species tolerates a wide range of soils once established.

directions: Introduced from China in the 1840s and the parent of dwarf and variegated selections such as 'Bronxensis' and 'Kumson', Forsythia viridissima is distinguished from the more common border forsythia hybrids by its upright, less arching habit and distinctive green, square-angled young stems that remain colorful through winter. Clusters of narrow-petaled, primrose-yellow flowers open along the bare stems in early to mid-spring, generally a shade paler and slightly later-blooming than F. x intermedia selections. The glossy, dark green summer foliage often holds later into fall than other forsythias before dropping. Prune immediately after flowering, removing a portion of the oldest canes at the base each year to keep the upright form open and floriferous.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
